chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Muhammad ibn Hafsh from al-Husayn ibn Khalid, and it was narrated by Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Muhammad ibn Ashyam from al-Husayn ibn Khalid, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) and said, 'We have narrated a hadith from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that I would like to hear from you.' He said, 'What is it?' I said, 'It reached me that he said regarding a man who cut off the head of a dead man: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said, 'Indeed, Allah has made sacred the body of a deceased Muslim what He made sacred from him while alive. So whoever does to the dead man what would constitute violation of the life of the living, upon him is the blood money.' He said, 'Abu Abdillah was truthful. Thus the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said.'

I said, 'If one cuts off the head of a dead man, or splits his belly, or does to him an act that constitutes violation of the life of the living, is the penalty upon him the full blood money of a soul?' He said, 'No.' Then he pointed to me with his little finger and said, 'This one has no blood money.' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Do you consider it the blood money of a soul?' I said, 'No.' He said, 'You are truthful.'

I said to him, 'What is the blood money of this if his head is cut off while he is dead?' He said, 'Its blood money is the blood money of the fetus in its mother's womb before the soul is breathed into it, and that is one hundred dinars.' I remained silent and was pleased with his answer. He said, 'Why do you not exhaust your inquiry?' I said, 'I do not have more to ask than what you have answered, unless there is something I do not know.'

He said, 'The blood money of the fetus, when its mother is struck and it falls from her womb before the soul is breathed into it, is one hundred dinars, and it belongs to its heirs. And indeed, the blood money of this one (the dead man whose head is cut off) if his head is cut off or his belly split, is not for his heirs; rather, it is for him alone, distinct from the heirs.'

I said, 'What is the difference between the two?' He said, 'The fetus is anticipated, and its benefit is hoped for, whereas this one has passed and his benefit has gone. So when he is mutilated after his death, his blood money becomes due to him specifically because of that mutilation, not for others. It is used on his behalf and acts are done with it from the doors of righteousness and goodness, such as charity or otherwise.'

I said, 'If a man intends to dig a grave for him to wash him in, and another man rushes into the hole being dug, and is buried with him, and his hand slips and strikes his belly and splits it, what is upon him?' He said, 'If it is thus, it is an error (mistake), and its expiation is freeing a slave, or fasting for two consecutive months, or feeding sixty poor people, a mud for each poor person, with the mud of the Prophet (peace be upon him).'

key_terms.اجْتِيَاحُ نَفْسِ الْحَيِّ: Violation of the life of the living
key_terms.مُدّ: A specific measure of volume for food

ai.seo_question: What is the blood money for cutting off the head of a dead Muslim according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfarayini’s chain in al-Istibsar clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between the sanctity of the living body and the residual honor of the deceased, establishing that mutilation incurs a fixed compensation (100 dinars) rather than full blood money. Imam al-Rida (AS) explains that this specific penalty belongs to the deceased personally to be spent on their behalf, reflecting the principle that the deceased retains a legal personality for posthumous rights. The narration further differentiates between intentional mutilation and accidental injury during burial rites, linking the latter to the standard expiation (kaffarah) for unintentional killing.
